patterns.name: Top-K via Bounded Heap
patterns.explanation: Maintain a min-heap of size K; for each new element, push it and pop the smallest if the heap exceeds K. After the scan, the heap holds the K largest elements. Symmetric for top-K smallest.
patterns.when_to_use: Kth Largest Element, Top K Frequent Elements, K Closest Points to Origin, Top K Frequent Words. Anywhere you'd otherwise sort all N elements just to keep K.
patterns.intuition: Sorting is O(N log N); a size-K heap is O(N log K), much better when K ≪ N. The 'opposite polarity' is the trick: to keep top-K largest, use a *min*-heap so the smallest of the K can be evicted in O(log K).
common_pitfalls: Using a max-heap to find top-K largest — works but is O(N log N)
Pushing then popping in the wrong order, returning K-1 elements
Custom comparator inverted (most languages default to min-heap)
Tie-breaking by insertion order incorrectly
patterns.complexity_signature: O(N log K) time, O(K) space

patterns.name: K-Way Merge
patterns.explanation: Merge K sorted streams into one in O(N log K) by maintaining a min-heap of size K, where each entry is the smallest unconsumed element of one stream. Pop the smallest, advance its source, and push the next.
patterns.when_to_use: Merge K Sorted Lists, Smallest Range Covering K Lists, Find K Pairs with Smallest Sums, Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix.
patterns.intuition: If each stream is sorted, the global minimum is one of the K stream-fronts. A heap of K stream-fronts gives the global min in O(log K), then advance that one stream and repeat.
common_pitfalls: Forgetting to push only the next element (not the entire remaining list)
Storing tuples in the wrong order so the comparator sorts on the wrong field
Not handling exhausted streams (skip when nothing left)
Using a flat sort O(N log N) when O(N log K) is required
patterns.complexity_signature: O(N log K) time, O(K) space

patterns.name: Two Heaps for Running Median
patterns.explanation: Maintain a max-heap (lower half) and a min-heap (upper half) such that their sizes differ by at most 1. The median is the top of the larger heap, or the average of the two tops if equal-sized.
patterns.when_to_use: Find Median from Data Stream, Sliding Window Median, IPO (sort of), problems where you need 'median of all numbers seen so far' updated as numbers arrive.
patterns.intuition: Splitting the sorted-so-far data at the median makes both halves accessible in O(log N) per insertion. Rebalancing keeps the median always at the top of one or both heaps.
common_pitfalls: Letting the size invariant drift — must rebalance after every insert
Forgetting to handle the very first insert (empty heaps)
Sliding-window median: removing arbitrary elements from a heap requires lazy deletion or a multi-set
Using one heap (sorted list) and getting O(N log N) per insert
patterns.complexity_signature: O(log N) per insert, O(1) per query

patterns.name: Scheduling / Earliest-Available with Heap
patterns.explanation: Use a min-heap to always pick the next available slot or the resource that becomes free earliest. Captures 'always pick the next earliest event' as a primitive.
patterns.when_to_use: Meeting Rooms II, Task Scheduler, Reorganize String, Single-Threaded CPU, Process Tasks Using Servers, Minimum Number of Refueling Stops.
patterns.intuition: When you must process events in a non-trivial order driven by 'next available time' or 'next deadline', a min-heap is the cleanest data structure: it always reveals the next event in O(log N).
common_pitfalls: Forgetting to handle the case where no resource is available (must advance time)
Mixing 'sort by start time' with 'heap by end time' incorrectly
Tie-breaking ambiguities (which task wins when two are simultaneously available)
Inserting future events too eagerly and corrupting the order
patterns.complexity_signature: O(N log N) time, O(N) space

patterns.name: Generic Priority Queue
patterns.explanation: Heap as a generic priority queue with custom priorities — for problems that need 'process the most/least important item next', without a specific shape like top-K or k-way merge.
patterns.when_to_use: Connect Sticks with Minimum Cost, Last Stone Weight, Furthest Building You Can Reach, Maximize Capital, Minimum Cost to Hire K Workers, Minimum Number of Operations to Reinitialize a Permutation.
patterns.intuition: When greedy says 'pick the best item next', and 'best' changes after each operation, a priority queue makes the greedy step efficient. Often combined with a sorted preprocessing step.
common_pitfalls: Forgetting to push back the modified result (e.g., merging two stones returns one new stone)
Confusing 'priority' direction (min vs. max)
Storing primitives directly when objects with multiple fields are needed
Re-heapifying manually instead of using language built-ins

patterns.name: Heap Inside Dijkstra-Shape Algorithms
patterns.explanation: Many graph-shaped problems extract 'minimum-distance unvisited node' repeatedly — a min-heap of `(distance, node)` makes each extraction O(log V). The pattern generalizes beyond shortest path to any best-first search on a weighted graph.
patterns.when_to_use: Network Delay Time, Cheapest Flights Within K Stops, Path with Minimum Effort, Swim in Rising Water, Minimum Cost to Make at Least One Valid Path. Any 'minimum sum/max/effort path' problem.
patterns.intuition: Best-first search with a min-heap is Dijkstra's algorithm; pop the closest unvisited node, relax neighbors, push updated distances. Lazy deletion lets you ignore stale entries cheaply.
common_pitfalls: Pushing a fresh entry on every relaxation without skipping stale ones
Using BFS on weighted graphs
Negative edges break Dijkstra — use Bellman–Ford instead
Storing nodes only and recomputing distances on each pop
patterns.complexity_signature: O((V + E) log V) time, O(V) space
